domain.title: Testing and reliability
domain.summary: Gaining confidence that code works before shipping, and keeping it working — observably and recoverably — once it runs.

concepts.title: Unit, integration, and end-to-end tests
concepts.summary: Different test scopes buy different confidence at different costs; choosing the boundary is a design decision.

related.boundary: Whether a test can fail, and fails reliably, maps there; which scope a test exercises maps here.

learningObjectives: Classify a test by the boundary it exercises
Explain what a given test would and would not catch
Choose the cheapest test scope that covers a specific risk
recognitionSignals: new tests or suites that start a real server, database, or test container
HTTP-level tests that drive routes through the app (e.g. supertest, httpx TestClient)
browser automation suites (Playwright, Cypress, Selenium)
test runner configuration that splits unit and integration suites or tags tests by scope
misconceptionPatterns: Believing end-to-end tests are always the best choice because they are the most realistic, so every edge case should be tested through the full stack
Assuming passing unit tests on both sides mean the components agree on the contract between them (payload shape, status codes, schema)
Believing a test's label (unit or integration) rather than what it actually executes determines what failures it can catch

concepts.title: Test doubles
concepts.summary: Mocks, stubs, fakes, and spies replace real dependencies in tests, trading realism for speed and control.
learningObjectives: Explain what a given test double lets the test control or verify (canned responses, recorded calls, a working substitute)
Identify tests that pass only because a mock diverges from the real dependency
Decide when a fake or real dependency is better than a mock
recognitionSignals: module or dependency mocking calls (vi.mock, jest.mock, unittest.mock.patch, gomock)
HTTP interception or mocked clients and database layers (msw, nock, responses)
in-memory fake implementations of repositories, queues, or clocks
assertions on how many times or with what arguments a mock was called
misconceptionPatterns: Believing a heavily mocked test verifies integration behavior
Believing that verifying a mock was called proves the feature works, even when the outcome (return value, stored state) could be checked directly
Assuming a hand-written mock's responses still match the real dependency after that dependency changes
Believing a test still exercises real logic after the code under test has itself been mocked or stubbed

concepts.title: Logs, metrics, and traces
concepts.summary: Structured logs, metrics, and traces let you understand what production is doing without attaching a debugger.
learningObjectives: Explain what a structured log line should contain to be useful in an incident
Distinguish when to use a log, a metric, or a trace
Identify logging that leaks sensitive data or is too noisy to use
recognitionSignals: structured logger calls with contextual fields (pino, winston, structlog, slog)
request or correlation IDs attached to logs or propagated in headers
metrics counters, histograms, or timers
tracing spans or OpenTelemetry instrumentation
error reporting SDK calls such as Sentry.captureException
misconceptionPatterns: Believing logs are internal, so it is safe to log tokens, passwords, or full request bodies
Believing more log lines always improve debuggability
Believing counting or rate questions are best answered by searching logs rather than recording a metric
Assuming unbounded values such as user IDs or raw URLs are fine as metric labels

concepts.title: Timeouts
concepts.summary: A timeout bounds how long code waits on something that may never answer, turning a hang into a handleable failure.

related.boundary: Deciding whether and how to try again maps there; bounding a single wait maps here.
Ambiguous outcomes across services and reconciliation map there.

learningObjectives: Identify outbound calls with no timeout
Explain how a slow dependency without timeouts can exhaust a service
Design timeout budgets across nested calls
recognitionSignals: server-side calls to third-party APIs or internal services with no timeout or abort signal
AbortController, AbortSignal.timeout, or HTTP client timeout options
database statement, lock, or connection-acquire timeouts
Promise.race or equivalents (context.WithTimeout, asyncio.wait_for) used to bound a wait
misconceptionPatterns: Believing HTTP clients have sensible default timeouts
Believing Promise.race against a timer cancels the slower operation, when it keeps running and holding resources
Assuming aborting a request on the client stops work already running on the server or in the database
Believing an inner call's timeout can safely exceed the outer request's deadline because the caller will keep waiting

concepts.title: Failure recovery
concepts.summary: When multi-step or background work fails partway, making the resulting state visible and recoverable: explicit failed states, bounded retries that end in a dead-letter or manual path, safe resumption, and honestly degraded responses.

related.boundary: Consistency across services (outbox, sagas, reconciliation) maps there; recovering failed work inside one application maps here.

learningObjectives: Trace what state a workflow is left in when it fails at each step
Compare retrying, dead-lettering, and failing fast for a given failure
Design a recovery path for work that fails permanently
recognitionSignals: background job or queue consumer configuration with max attempts or retry limits
dead-letter queues, failed-job tables, or manual replay tooling
status moved to a failed or needs-attention state when a workflow step errors
catch branches that return cached, partial, or default responses when a dependency is down
circuit breaker or fallback wrappers around dependency calls
misconceptionPatterns: Assuming a failed job leaves no partial state
Believing enough retries will eventually succeed, so permanent failures never need a separate path
Believing silent fallbacks are safer than making degraded behavior visible to users and operators

concepts.title: Tests that can fail
concepts.summary: A test is evidence only if it would fail when the behavior breaks and gives the same result on every run; weak assertions and nondeterminism turn tests into noise.
learningObjectives: Predict whether a test would fail if the behavior it describes were broken
Identify sources of nondeterminism in a test: wall-clock time, randomness, execution order, shared state, and un-awaited async work
Explain why a regression test should be seen failing before the fix is applied
recognitionSignals: assertions that only check truthiness, that no error was thrown, or that a snapshot exists
async expectations or assertions that are not awaited
tests that read the current time, random values, or the network without controlling them (fake timers, seeded randomness)
retries, skips, or longer timeouts added to make a test pass
shared fixtures or database state not reset between tests
misconceptionPatterns: Believing high code coverage means the important behavior is tested
Believing a passing test is evidence of correctness even though it has never been seen to fail
Treating a flaky test as noise to retry or skip rather than a sign of a race or hidden dependency
Assuming tests run in a fixed order with isolated state
